senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the rank “absolute within the relative” (偏中正) names the absolute or upright disclosed within the relative or differentiated, reversing the nesting of “relative within the absolute” while remaining paired with it in explanations and verse sequences. Caoshan Benji glosses the rank as leaving affairs and entering principle. The Eyes of Humans and Devas transmits the same affairs-to-principle gloss in its Five Ranks account. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives the rank a sea-cloud, sacred-peak, returning-traveler, and mirror image. Langting Ting pairs it with a yellow bird carrying spring news. Juelang Daosheng associates it with a western circle and lesser yin, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies the same shout as this rank when it is silent right where it occurs. Tianran Hanshi reports Dongshan's old-woman-and-mirror stanza and answers it with another mirror verse; the varied images illustrate rather than define the relation.
senses.Note: Seven exact witnesses in seven independent works support the reverse nested relation paired with “relative within the absolute”; the target uses conventional absolute-relative terminology, with older upright-partial wording retained as alternates.

senses.PreferredTarget: birth and death is the great matter
senses.Explanation: The formula says that birth and death is the great matter: the records make it an urgent reason to seek clarification, and several directly explain it as not knowing where birth comes from or where death goes. Dahui Zonggao calls not knowing one's coming the greatness of birth and not knowing one's destination the greatness of death, and names that condition with the formula. Tianru Weize gives the same paired explanation, while Xueyan Zuqin urges listeners to take it as a matter of unsurpassed weight and get it clear. Yuanwu Keqin describes declaring this great matter and one's own affair still unclear as the proper initial reason for approaching an established lineage instructor. Zhongfeng Mingben rebukes people who carry the words in their mouths while hunting a phrase from old paper. Dufeng Xingjian says neither saying nor knowing it is enough, and Shending Yunwai Ze says it cannot be finished through oral proof or acceptance in thought. The entry therefore records urgency, definition, and corrective use without treating repetition of the slogan as its resolution.
senses.Note: The exact formula occurs 401 times in 153 allowlisted files. Seven selected witnesses in seven independent works establish one phrase; the reordered family “great matter of birth and death” is tracked as a related form rather than substituted into exact evidence.

senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, coming from within the absolute (正中來) names a movement from the upright or correct position; Caoshan describes it as words within no-words, without setting up rank or falling to either side. Caoshan Benji explains the label through coming from the correct position and gives examples of speech within no-speech. Hongzhi Zhengjue's verse pictures a great fish shedding its shell and taking the bird path, while an unnamed monastic later asks Fenyang Shanzhao for the rank and receives the image of lotuses opening on dry ground. Langting Ting pairs the rank with partridge calls and opening flowers. Juelang Daosheng later explains it through a ruler at the highest point, Yongjue Yuanxian gives a midnight plum opening against snow, and Ruibai Mingxue classifies a shout free of names and words as this rank. These changing images and schemata illustrate one named relation rather than establish separate senses.
senses.Note: The exact rank label occurs 320 times in 96 allowlisted files. Seven witnesses in seven independent works support one Five Ranks relation; later diagrammatic systems remain attributed examples rather than the lexical definition.

senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, arrival within integration (兼中到) is the fifth named relation. Dongshan’s verse places it outside the opposition of existence and nonexistence; later records repeatedly describe distinctions as exhausted or integrated. Dongshan Liangjie begins the fifth-rank verse by saying it falls into neither existence nor nonexistence. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives it a dawn verse, while an unnamed monastic asks Fenyang Shanzhao for it and receives images of a weaving jade woman and a drumming stone man. Langting Ting uses a returning cuckoo, Juelang Daosheng offers a later black-white diagram, Yongjue Yuanxian says affairs and principle are both gone, and Ruibai Mingxue applies it to a shout after holy and ordinary, subject and object, and existence and nonexistence are exhausted. These remain attributed illustrations of one rank.

senses.Explanation: To be made into one piece is to become continuous rather than divided by time, motion and stillness, arising and perishing, or subject and object. The records apply the phrase across sustained inquiry and all twelve periods of daily activity. Zhongfeng Mingben places it after long continuity; Tianyin Yuanxiu requires it through all twelve periods of the day; Weian Deran pairs it with arising and perishing becoming one and motion and stillness not being two. Ruibai Mingxue says subject and object both disappear. A later record quotes Xiangyan Zhixian saying that it took forty years. Yuanwu Keqin uses the phrase as a name for the one-colour side, while Zhongfeng elsewhere rejects calling a consciously recognized silver mountain and iron wall by this name. The negative witness blocks the idea that one merely imagines a separate object and pounds it together.
senses.Note: The exact phrase occurs 340 times in 153 allowlisted files. Seven exact witnesses across seven independent works support one continuity/unification sense; the close form “make into one piece” remains related rather than counted here.
